newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Broaddus--recent inflation data encouraging.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Broaddus--recent inflation data encouraging.

text.p: Alfred Broaddus, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, on Wednesday called recent data on U.S. inflation encouraging but reiterated the need for the central bank to work toward price stability.
"The recent inflation reports have...been encouraging," Broaddus said in a speech at the University of North Carolina at Pembroke.

The U.S. Labor Department's report on the consumer price index for September showed the index up by 0.3 percent both overall and in the so-called "core" rate, which excludes volatile food and energy components.
That was higher than the 0.1 percent increase recorded for August. But Broaddus said: "we all know monthly numbers bounce around a lot."
Broaddus highlighted the fact that the core CPI is up 2.7 percent over the last year, which he said was "a quite moderate rate of growth."

In his speech, the Richmond Fed chief reiterated the need to work toward price stability, which Alan Greenspan, the central bank's chairman, has described as a condition where inflation is no longer a factor in economic decisions made by businesses and consumers.
Broaddus said the current inflation rate of around three percent was "not good enough." He suggested pushing the rate down toward two percent and "holding it there for the long haul."

Turning to recent trends in economic growth, Broaddus noted that gross domestic product growth decelerated sharply in the third quarter to an annual rate of 2.2 percent after "hefty" growth of 4.7 percent in the second quarter.

However, he said: "My own view is that this is a happy outcome because it tends to support the current predictions of the majority of economic forecasters that the economy is slowing to a more sustainable growth rate."
Despite the slowing, Broaddus described the level of economic activity overall as "quite high."

"We see this in a lot of different industries, particularly in labour markets," Broaddus said. He added that labour markets were tight across the country in various sectors and among various categories of skill levels.

The unemployment rate now stands at 5.2 percent. Broaddus said that many economists view a jobless rate in the region of 5-1/2 percent as "full employment," or the lowest level of unemployment that can be sustained without triggering higher inflation.
Some economists have argued that structural changes in the economy may mean that the old rules about inflation have changed to a point where it is less of a risk.
Broaddus said he was "suspicious" of such theories.
